narrative.text: The Chinese-language cover of the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework for the sharing of influenza viruses and access to vaccines and other benefits, with the title text repeated.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The Chinese title page of the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework, repeating the cover title.
The cataloguing and copyright page of the Chinese edition, with English WHO library cataloguing data and subject headings and Chinese rights, permissions and disclaimer notices.

The first page of the table of contents of the Chinese PIP Framework, listing resolution WHA64.5, the principles, objectives, scope, definitions, the virus-sharing system and the start of the benefit-sharing system.

Continues the Chinese table of contents, listing benefit-sharing sections such as stockpiles, tiered pricing, technology transfer and financing, governance and review, and the annexes containing the two standard material transfer agreements and laboratory terms of reference.

Presents resolution WHA64.5 of the Sixty-fourth World Health Assembly (24 May 2011), which welcomes the work of the open-ended working group and adopts the Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework and its annexes. It urges Member States to implement and resource the Framework and calls on stakeholders to prioritize it.
Concludes resolution WHA64.5 by asking the Director-General, with the Advisory Group, to implement, monitor and review the Framework and report progress to the Health Assembly every two years.

Begins the principles of the PIP Framework, recalling resolution WHA60.28 and the continuing risk of a pandemic with severe impact, particularly on developing countries. It sets out Member States' commitment to share H5N1 and other potentially pandemic influenza viruses and their benefits on an equal footing, rapidly and systematically, in line with the International Health Regulations (2005).

Continues the Framework's principles, recognizing WHO's leadership, countries' sovereign rights over biological resources, and the global strategy on public health, innovation and intellectual property. It notes concern about the limited and uneven distribution of influenza vaccine production capacity and refers to the WHO Global Pandemic Influenza Action Plan to increase vaccine supply.
Concludes the principles by recognizing the need to transfer vaccine, diagnostic and medicine technologies to developing countries and to create financing mechanisms for affordable, equitable access.

States the Framework's objective of improving pandemic influenza preparedness and response by strengthening the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System, to ensure fair, transparent and equitable sharing of viruses and access to vaccines and other benefits.

Defines the scope of the Framework as covering the sharing of H5N1 and other potentially pandemic influenza viruses and the resulting benefits, excluding seasonal influenza viruses and other pathogens in clinical specimens.

Begins the definitions section, defining PIP biological materials to include human clinical specimens, virus isolates, modified candidate vaccine viruses and certain RNA and cDNA. It also starts the list of other technical terms and gives a footnote on the operational exemption for non-commercial public health use.

Defines further technical terms, such as potency testing reagents, influenza virus of human pandemic potential, PIP candidate vaccine virus, clinical specimens, reference viruses and wild-type influenza viruses.

Defines the institutions and entities referred to in the Framework, including essential regulatory laboratories, manufacturers, national influenza centres, other authorized laboratories, WHO collaborating centres, H5 reference laboratories and the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System.

Completes the definitions with other terms, such as the Advisory Group, affected country, least developed countries, originating laboratory and originating Member State, the influenza virus traceability mechanism and the PIP vaccine and antiviral stockpiles.

Opens the section on the system for sharing H5N1 and other potentially pandemic viruses, under which Member States should rapidly provide PIP biological materials to WHO collaborating centres or H5 reference laboratories, thereby consenting to onward transfer under the standard material transfer agreements. It also allows bilateral sharing if WHO laboratories are given priority and begins the provisions on sharing genetic sequence data within the network.

Notes efforts to share genetic sequence data through public databases such as GenBank and GISAID, while recognizing that some countries consider publishing such data sensitive, and asks the Director-General to find a process for resolving these issues. It then describes an electronic traceability mechanism for tracking PIP biological materials, which may be temporarily modified during a pandemic emergency.
Specifies that SMTA 1 covers transfers of PIP biological materials within the WHO surveillance network, while SMTA 2 will be concluded with entities outside the network.

Opens the PIP benefit-sharing system, under which Member States and WHO, with manufacturers and researchers, should provide all countries with surveillance, risk assessment and early warning, and prioritize benefits such as antivirals and vaccines for developing and affected countries based on public health risk and need. It also mentions building countries' capacity and begins the section on WHO's coordination of pandemic preparedness and response under the International Health Regulations.

Notes WHO's role in promoting fair, equitable and transparent allocation of scarce resources such as vaccines, antivirals and diagnostics during a pandemic. It then covers pandemic risk assessment, with network laboratories sharing analysis reports with originating countries, and the provision of candidate vaccine viruses to manufacturers and laboratories without preference, subject to biosafety rules.

Covers the provision of free diagnostic reagents and test kits to national influenza centres and of reagents for vaccine potency testing to regulators and manufacturers. It also describes building laboratory and surveillance capacity and strengthening regulatory capacity in developing countries.

Asks Member States to share public information on regulatory approvals of pandemic vaccines, diagnostics and medicines, and describes efforts to sustain an antiviral stockpile through donations. It then sets out the WHO PIP vaccine stockpile of an initial 150 million doses of H5N1 vaccine, 50 million for affected countries to contain early outbreaks and 100 million to be distributed per capita to developing countries once a pandemic starts.

Asks Member States to urge manufacturers to donate vaccine to the PIP stockpile and describes how the Director-General will manage its size, use and deployment, including possible pre-pandemic use and financing if donations fall short. It also covers vaccine for developing countries in inter-pandemic periods and asks that part of each pandemic vaccine production run be reserved for developing countries.

Calls for tiered pricing of pandemic vaccines and antivirals according to country income, with attention to least developed countries. It then covers technology transfer under the Global Pandemic Influenza Action Plan, including new production facilities and sharing of know-how, and encourages countries seeking production technology to first study the burden of seasonal influenza.

Sets out sustainable and innovative financing for the PIP benefit-sharing system, under which manufacturers using the WHO network pay an annual partnership contribution equal to 50% of the network's running costs from 2012, shared fairly among companies. A footnote puts the network's 2010 operating costs at about US$ 56.5 million, and other provisions support the global action plan through 2015.
Urges Member States to support access to adjuvant technology with stronger vaccine safety monitoring and to keep funding laboratory and surveillance capacity in developing countries.

Opens the governance and review section, explaining that the Health Assembly oversees the Framework with the Director-General and an independent Advisory Group of international experts, each with defined roles. It describes the Advisory Group's function of monitoring the WHO surveillance network and the trust-based system needed to implement the Framework.

Describes the Advisory Group's composition of 18 members, three from each WHO region, with balance between developed and developing countries, and its annual report on technical capacity, operations and preparedness priorities of the network. It also states that terms of reference for network laboratories will follow the guiding principles in Annex 4.

Explains that the Director-General will periodically review laboratory terms of reference and may suspend or withdraw WHO designation for serious breaches of the terms or the material transfer agreements. It sets out monitoring and reporting on the Framework, including the partnership contribution, and plans a review by 2016 with recommendations to the Health Assembly in 2017.
A blank page with no extracted text.
A divider page bearing the heading 'Annexes'.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Annex 1, Standard Material Transfer Agreement 1 for transfers within the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System, opens by limiting the parties to WHO-designated or recognized influenza laboratories and defining provider and recipient. It states that the agreement covers PIP biological materials as defined in the Framework.

Sets out general provisions of SMTA 1 and the provider's obligations, such as fulfilling network terms of reference, handling materials under biosafety guidance and transferring them onward within the network on the same terms. Transfers outside the network require the recipient to have signed SMTA 2, and the recipient's obligations begin.

Requires recipients under SMTA 1 to log transfers in the traceability mechanism, involve scientists from originating laboratories, especially in developing countries, in research and publications, and acknowledge their contributions. It states that neither party should seek intellectual property rights on the materials and sets out dispute settlement through consultation and, if needed, referral to the Director-General.

Covers the remaining terms of SMTA 1: no warranty on the safety or quality of the materials, a term running to 31 December 2021 with automatic extension to 2031, acceptance by laboratories through their terms of reference, and no need for a signed document unless requested.

Annex 2, Standard Material Transfer Agreement 2 for recipients outside the WHO network, names WHO and the recipient as parties and covers PIP biological materials. It requires recipients to choose commitments according to their nature and capacity, starting with options for vaccine and antiviral manufacturers.

Lists the benefit-sharing options under SMTA 2, such as donating or reserving at affordable prices at least 10% of real-time pandemic vaccine production, donating or reserving antiviral courses, and licensing technology to developing-country manufacturers on fair or royalty-free terms. It also lists options for diagnostics manufacturers and support for laboratory capacity, noting flexibility in negotiating the 5–20% range.

Completes the SMTA 2 commitment options and lists further measures recipients should consider, such as donating vaccines, antivirals, devices or diagnostics, tiered pricing and technology transfer. It also sets out recipients' biosafety and acknowledgement duties, permitted exchanges with other SMTA holders and binding arbitration for disputes.

Covers the remaining SMTA 2 articles, preserving WHO's privileges and immunities and leaving use of names, warranties, duration, termination, force majeure and applicable law to be agreed, followed by signature blocks.

Annex 3, the terms of reference of the PIP Advisory Group, recalls the 2007 interim statement that called for a fair, transparent virus- and benefit-sharing mechanism and an advisory mechanism to monitor it. It begins listing the group's functions of monitoring, assessing and reporting on the Framework's components.

Lists the areas the Advisory Group monitors, such as virus sharing, the traceability mechanism, laboratory capacity, benefit sharing and use of contributions, and its duties to evaluate the Framework, advise the Director-General and report annually through the Executive Board to the Health Assembly.

Describes Advisory Group membership of 18 experts, three from each WHO region, serving three-year staggered terms with a chair and vice-chair elected for two years. It also covers working methods, confidentiality rules and the resources the Director-General will provide.

Annex 4, the guiding principles for terms of reference of WHO network laboratories handling H5N1 and other potentially pandemic viruses, explains that roles vary by laboratory type. The principles require activities to follow the Framework and SMTA, support WHO, report results and involve scientists from originating countries, especially developing countries, in research and publications.

Completes the guiding principles, requiring network laboratories to support global emergency response, share PIP materials through the traceability mechanism, submit gene sequences to GISAID, GenBank or similar databases, and acknowledge originating laboratories.

Annex 5 opens the terms of reference for WHO collaborating centres working with PIP biological materials, describing the network's four types of laboratories coordinated by WHO's Global Influenza Programme. It explains that core terms of reference are minimum requirements and that collective exchange of materials and data underpins pandemic risk assessment.

Reproduces the guiding principles agreed by the intergovernmental meeting that govern all network laboratories, such as compliance with the Framework and SMTA, support to WHO, timely reporting and involving scientists from originating countries.

Completes the reproduced guiding principles and begins the core terms of reference for WHO influenza collaborating centres, which must work under WHO coordination, use the traceability mechanism, exchange materials promptly and have biosafety level 3 facilities.

Continues the general duties of WHO collaborating centres, such as serving as WHO technical resources, acknowledging originating laboratories, working closely with national influenza centres and reporting unusual findings. It also covers providing expertise to help developing countries respond to outbreaks and advising the network on diagnostic methods.

Lists laboratory analyses WHO collaborating centres must perform on potentially pandemic viruses, including diagnosis, subtyping, virus isolation, detailed antigenic and genetic analysis, sharing and uploading gene sequences and antiviral susceptibility testing. It also covers selecting and updating reference viruses and candidate vaccine viruses.

Requires collaborating centres to develop and distribute diagnostic reagents to national influenza centres and to share specimens and viruses under SMTA 1 with other WHO laboratories, regulatory laboratories and coordinated programmes. It also covers maintaining and distributing reference viruses and antisera for non-commercial use.

Sets the research and publication duties of collaborating centres, requiring involvement of scientists from originating countries and proper acknowledgement following editorial guidelines, and notes that specific terms of reference add functions based on each centre's expertise.

Opens the terms of reference for national influenza centres working with PIP biological materials, with the same background on the WHO network and its four types of laboratories and an introduction to the guiding principles.

Reproduces the guiding principles for network laboratories in the national influenza centre terms of reference, covering compliance with the Framework and SMTA, support to WHO, reporting and sharing of materials and gene sequences.

Completes the guiding principles and begins the core terms of reference for national influenza centres, which are designated by health ministries and recognized by WHO. Their general duties include working under WHO coordination, logging transfers in the traceability mechanism and following the SMTA, and their laboratory duties begin with collecting specimens from suspected cases.

Lists further laboratory duties of national influenza centres, such as testing specimens, sending unidentified viruses to a WHO collaborating centre or H5 reference laboratory within one week with relevant data, attending training and strengthening national surveillance. It also covers advising other national laboratories and research duties on involving and acknowledging originating scientists.

Opens the terms of reference for WHO H5 reference laboratories working with PIP biological materials, with background on the WHO network, the minimum core requirements for designation and an introduction to the guiding principles.

Reproduces the guiding principles for network laboratories within the H5 reference laboratory terms of reference, on following the Framework and SMTA, supporting WHO, reporting results and sharing materials and gene sequences.

Begins the core terms of reference for WHO H5 reference laboratories, which must work under WHO coordination, meet WHO criteria for confirming human H5 infection, log transfers in the traceability mechanism and follow the Framework's SMTA. Their laboratory duties start with advising clinics and hospitals on safe specimen collection, storage and shipment.

Lists further duties of H5 reference laboratories, including accurate diagnosis and subtyping of H5 and other potentially pandemic viruses, outbreak support, routine sharing of specimens and isolates with WHO collaborating centres and prompt sharing of gene sequences. It closes with research duties to involve and acknowledge scientists from originating countries.

Opens the terms of reference for essential regulatory laboratories working with PIP biological materials, with background on the WHO network and the minimum core requirements these laboratories must meet individually or collectively, with specific terms possibly agreed with WHO and industry.

Reproduces the guiding principles for network laboratories within the essential regulatory laboratory terms of reference, covering compliance with the Framework and SMTA, support to WHO, reporting, emergency support and sharing of PIP materials.

Completes the guiding principles and lists the core general duties of essential regulatory laboratories, such as advising WHO on selecting H5N1 and other potentially pandemic viruses for vaccines and helping with vaccine aspects of preparedness plans. Their laboratory duties begin with storing and expanding representative viruses for vaccine development.

Lists further laboratory duties of essential regulatory laboratories, including developing and characterizing candidate vaccine viruses at WHO's request, preparing and calibrating reference reagents for vaccine standardization and distributing them under SMTA 1. It ends with research duties on involving and acknowledging collaborators.
A blank page with no extracted text.
The back cover of the Chinese edition of the PIP Framework, with its ISBN and WHO's Geneva address.
